candidateRows: Absolute divine simplicity denies distinct intrinsic compositions in God, including substance and essence, subject and attributes, agent and action, essence and existence, act and potency, and form and matter.
This taxonomy defines the distinct simplicity commitments that organize the subsequent arguments and objections throughout the debate.
After the host asks for Joe's largest problems, Joe first establishes the forms of composition classical theists exclude before objections are assessed.
The various traditional compositions should be assessed individually, while their common rationale is that Aristotelian metaphysics understands them as divisions between actuality and potentiality.
The move supplies the metaphysical framework connecting the enumerated compositions and explains why pure actuality motivates excluding each from God.
Joe's preceding taxonomy of the kinds of composition excluded from God
Chris accepts most of Joe's taxonomy, qualifies the essence-existence claim against a pantheistic reading, and unifies the distinctions through act and potency.

Divine simplicity does not identify creaturely power with creaturely knowledge; analogous predication says that God's single essence is like each perfection without containing really distinct properties.
This directly addresses an apparent incoherence in attribute identity and supplies analogy as the conceptual mechanism by which the pro side avoids it.
The host's challenge that omniscience and omnipotence cannot intelligibly be the same property
In response to a question about identical divine attributes, Chris distinguishes univocal creaturely properties from analogous predication of God's one essence.
A part can be characterized as any positive ontological item intrinsic to a subject yet distinct from it, making absolute simplicity the thesis that anything intrinsic to God is identical to God.
The characterization establishes the operative criterion for parts and therefore fixes what later objections must show to challenge absolute divine simplicity.
Before presenting objections, Joe formalizes the debate's notion of a part and relates it to traditional formulations that whatever is in God is God.

Simplicity requires everything intrinsic to God to be really identical with God, while permitting grounded conceptual distinctions and contingent extrinsic predications that concern creatures rather than intrinsic changes in God.
The intrinsic-real qualification defines the pro position's scope and is essential to its treatment of divine attributes, change, contingency, and knowledge.
Joe's formulation that anything intrinsic to God is identical to God
Chris refines Joe's definition with the word really, distinguishes conceptual from real difference, and exempts extrinsic predicates from simplicity's prohibition.
Divine aseity motivates simplicity because any intrinsic parts distinct from God would make God's being or intrinsic properties depend upon something that is not God.
This is a direct positive argument for divine simplicity from God's radical metaphysical independence, one of the doctrine's principal classical motivations.
Chris begins the motivations section by connecting God's status as metaphysically ultimate and independent with the exclusion of distinct intrinsic parts.

Aseity need not entail simplicity because dependence may be merely counterfactual, God may ground his own parts, strong aseity may conflict with Trinitarian multiplicity, or aseity may exclude only dependence on what is outside God.
These alternatives challenge the key inference from divine independence to absence of intrinsic differentiation and supply several routes for rejecting that inference.
Chris's argument that distinct intrinsic parts would compromise God's complete aseity
Joe answers the aseity motivation with four concise strategies distinguishing kinds of dependence and offering weaker or differently ordered metaphysical accounts.

The relevant dependence is explanatory rather than merely counterfactual, and priority monism fails because even if God grounded his parts, God could not ground the unifying fact that makes those parts one God.
The move concedes an irrelevant dependence notion while defending the aseity argument against priority monism through the load-bearing unity-of-parts objection.
Joe's counterfactual-dependence distinction and proposal that God could ground God's own parts
Chris narrows the aseity concern to metaphysical grounding and argues that a composite God's unity, rather than the isolated parts, would explain the one being.

Classical natural-theology arguments yield a purely actual first being, and because the relevant compositions contain actuality and potentiality, pure actuality entails the exclusion of composition in God.
This gives an independent positive route to divine simplicity by connecting the conclusion of classical arguments for God with the absence of potentiality and composition.
Chris uses Aquinas's First Way as an example of how a proof of an unmoved, purely actual source sets the stage for simplicity.
Trinitarianism and classical divine simplicity form an inconsistent tetrad if divine processions are positive ontological items intrinsic to but distinct from God.
The tetrad directly challenges whether classical divine simplicity can coexist coherently with Trinitarian persons and their asymmetric processions.
After introductory remarks that divine simplicity comprises several distinct debates, Joe opens the selected Trinitarian objection by laying out four jointly inconsistent commitments.
A Latin Trinitarian model preserves divine simplicity by identifying each person and procession with the divine nature while distinguishing persons through opposed relations.
This is the principal classical-theist answer to the alleged conflict between divine simplicity and the reality and distinction of the Trinitarian persons.
Joe's tetrad claiming that Trinitarian processions are positive intrinsic items distinct from God.
Chris concedes that social Trinitarian models conflict with simplicity, then argues that a Latin relational model avoids treating the persons as parts or additions to God.
The Son's asymmetric begottenness distinguishes the Son from the unbegotten Godhead, yielding an intrinsic item not strictly identical with God and therefore composition.
The objection targets the crucial relational-identity maneuver by arguing that asymmetric generation reinstates precisely the intrinsic distinction simplicity excludes.
Chris's claim that the persons are relations identical with the divine essence yet distinguished from one another.
Following discussion of why the Trinity has no strict creaturely analogue, Joe presses the asymmetry between the begotten Son and the unbegotten Godhead against Chris's model.
The Son is identical with his begottenness, while relational directedness distinguishes him from the Father without adding another positive ontological item to the divine essence.
The response directly defends relational identity against the asymmetry objection and explains why begottenness does not introduce composition into God.
Joe's argument that the Son's begottenness makes him intrinsically distinct from the unbegotten Godhead.
Chris answers that begottenness describes the Son insofar as he is directed toward the Father, whereas the Son considered absolutely is the divine essence itself.
In a possible world where God creates nothing, God's contingent knowledge must be intrinsic, making it a contingent accident in God and contradicting divine simplicity.
The argument directly alleges that divine freedom, omniscience, and the absence of accidents cannot jointly coexist with divine simplicity in an uncreated world.
After closing the Trinitarian exchange, Joe introduces a new aloneness argument: classical theism permits God alone, yet omniscience gives God contingent knowledge in that world.
God's existing alone does not entail that every property God then has is intrinsic, because aloneness itself can change through creation without any intrinsic change in God.
The counterexample attacks the inference on which the aloneness argument depends, namely that nothing can be extrinsic to God in a God-only possible world.
Joe's premise that any positive reality present when God exists alone must be intrinsic to God.
Chris first situates the objection within the traditional treatment of changing divine knowledge, then argues that relational properties may remain extrinsic even in an alone world.
Knowledge is extrinsic insofar as it entails truth, since a subject can cease knowing when external reality changes even if nothing intrinsic to the subject changes.
This factivity argument directly addresses contingent divine knowledge rather than properties generally and offers an independent defeat of the critic's intrinsic-knowledge premise.
Joe's claim that God's contingent knowledge in an alone world must constitute contingent intrinsic reality.
Chris uses a hypothetical lone creature who knows there are no dogs to argue that knowledge depends on externally varying truth and is therefore not wholly intrinsic.
The changing-knowledge argument allows extrinsic aspects of knowledge while still requiring a contingent intrinsic component in God for positive contingent truths.
This directly preserves Joe's earlier objection from Chris's appeal to the extrinsic character of truth and knowledge by clarifying what the objection actually requires.
Chris's claim that the factivity of knowledge makes all knowledge extrinsic and that aloneness supplies a counterexample.

After Chris argues that truth and therefore knowledge are extrinsic even for creatures, Joe clarifies that his premise does not require wholly intrinsic knowledge and defends a mixed intrinsic-extrinsic account.
If an omniscient God acquires and loses knowledge as contingent reality changes, then God has potentiality and classical divine simplicity is false.
This is a fully developed direct argument against classical theism, connecting temporal change, omniscience, potentiality, immutability, and divine simplicity.

Joe presents a formal act-potency argument, supports its first premise through classical accounts of timelessness and immutability, and supports its second through changing contingent truths and omniscience.
The act-potency argument equivocates between knowledge as an intrinsic ontological feature of God and knowledge as a partly extrinsic predication involving changing truths.
This is Chris's principal answer to the formal argument against divine simplicity and supplies an account of changing knowledge compatible with intrinsic divine immutability.
Joe's argument that changing omniscient knowledge entails potentiality in God and therefore falsifies divine simplicity.
Chris distinguishes predicables from real intrinsic properties, argues that truth contributes an extrinsic element to knowledge, and locates changes in what God knows entirely in the changing world.
Highly extrinsic accounts of divine knowledge risk ceasing to describe knowledge unless they explain what God's temporally changing dinosaur knowledge actually consists in.
The challenge presses the intelligibility of Chris's main reply at precisely the point where intrinsic divine reality is held constant while knowledge predications change.
Chris's claim that differences in God's knowledge can be exhausted by extrinsic differences in contingent reality.
Joe accepts that the debate turns on extrinsic models but asks what changing divine knowledge consists in, suggesting that the model may stretch the concept of knowledge beyond recognition.
God's knowledge includes an unchanging intrinsic intellect and causal efficacy, while the difference between temporally indexed items of knowledge is wholly extrinsic.
This concretely specifies the components of divine knowledge and directly answers the principal intelligibility challenge raised against the extrinsic-change defense.
Joe's challenge to explain what changing divine knowledge consists in under an extrinsic model.

Chris separates the intrinsic intellect and causal efficacy involved in each item of divine knowledge from the entirely extrinsic difference supplied by dinosaurs existing earlier and not existing now.
God could rationally choose to exist alone because his reasons may exceed human understanding, undiluted perfection may be preferable, or he may be self-sufficient.
The answer bears on divine freedom and the coherence of an alone-world scenario used throughout the central dispute over contingent creation and divine knowledge.
In response to an audience question about why God would ever be alone, Joe supplies skeptical-theist and substantive possible reasons for freely refraining from creation.
God can exist alone because creation adds no goodness to a perfectly good God or world and is instead a gratuitous act ordered to creatures and divine glory.
The argument connects divine freedom in creation with perfect goodness, self-sufficiency, and grace, addressing a major component of the debate's stated motion.
The audience's challenge asking why the God of classical theism would ever choose to exist alone.
Chris agrees that God can refrain from creation and argues that creation cannot improve God or total reality, so creating is gratuitous and for creatures rather than divine need.
God's love and power are identical with his being, while real Trinitarian distinctions are relational rather than absolute distinctions among intrinsic divine properties.
The answer directly addresses the compatibility of divine simplicity with distinct divine attributes and Trinitarian doctrine, both explicit components of the motion.
The audience question whether divine love and power are identical to God's being if distinctions in God lack independent reality.
Chris qualifies the claim that all distinctions in God are constructs, preserves real relational Trinitarian distinctions, and identifies divine love and power with God's being.
On the truthmaker account of divine simplicity, distinct true predications about God can differ in meaning while sharing God himself as their single truthmaker.
The account supplies a major metaphysical formulation of divine simplicity that explains multiple divine predications without positing multiple intrinsic constituents in God.
Joe notes interpretive debate about scriptural claims and then explains the truthmaker model, under which diverse predicates have different meanings but one divine truthmaker.
God can know what it is like to be a sinner without acquiring that knowledge by personally being a sinner.
The answer directly addresses whether classical omniscience can encompass creaturely experience without compromising divine perfection or requiring sinful experience.
The question challenges whether an omniscient God can know what being a sinner is like.
After confirming divine power to take vengeance, the respondent distinguishes knowing an experience from undergoing it and grounds divine knowledge in God's causal relation to creatures.
Disagreements about divine simplicity are largely derivative of more fundamental disagreements about metaphysics and the philosophy of nature.
The move identifies essence-existence composition, accidents, and creaturely metaphysics as the underlying framework governing judgments about composition in God.

In answering a request for introductory resources, Chris argues that readers should first settle prerequisite metaphysical questions before evaluating divine simplicity and then recommends primary and secondary works.
Trinitarian relations do not presuppose already constituted divine persons because the persons are identical with their subsistent relations.
This directly addresses the alleged incoherence between divine simplicity and three divine persons by explaining how personal distinction can consist in relations.
The audience objection asks how three subsistent relational persons are possible if God is simple.
Chris identifies the Father with paternity and the Spirit with the relevant relation of procession, arguing that these relations constitute rather than presuppose the persons.
The proposed account of subsistent Trinitarian relations is not possible given divine simplicity.
Although brief, the response directly rejects the pro side's attempted reconciliation of divine simplicity with distinct Trinitarian persons and relations.
Chris's preceding account identifies the divine persons with subsistent relations compatible with simplicity.
After acknowledging the preceding discussion, Joe says he cannot supply the requested reconciliation because he denies that the Trinitarian arrangement is possible under divine simplicity.
Extrinsic changes do not temporalize God because the relevant changing relations inhere in creatures rather than in God.
The response addresses a central coherence objection concerning divine knowledge of changing contingent reality while preserving simplicity, immutability, and atemporality.
The question argues that extrinsic relational changes may suffice to make the simple God temporal.
Chris locates changing God-world relations in creatures and illustrates the asymmetry through dinosaurs and divine knowledge, claiming the world conforms to God's mind rather than conversely.
